title: Problem Overview and History
content:
**Erdős Problem #226**: Is there an entire non-linear $f$ with $x \in \mathbb{Q} \Leftrightarrow f(x) \in \mathbb{Q}$?

**Status**: SOLVED (YES) by Barth-Schneider (1970)

The question goes beyond Stäckel's 1895 result that a transcendental entire function can map $\mathbb{Q}$ into $\mathbb{Q}$: Erdős required the biconditional. Barth and Schneider proved the much stronger result that for ANY countable dense $A, B \subset \mathbb{R}$, a transcendental entire $f$ with $f(A) = B$ exists. Their 1971 follow-up extended this to $\mathbb{C}$.
mathContext: $f : \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}$ entire, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}: x \in \mathbb{Q} \Leftrightarrow f(x) \in \mathbb{Q}$. Problem 2.31 in Hayman's 1974 collection [Ha74].

title: Entire Function Definitions
content:
Three key definitions:

- `IsEntire(f)` := `Differentiable ℂ f` — holomorphic on all of $\mathbb{C}$
- `IsTranscendental(f)` := `IsEntire f ∧ ¬∃ (n : ℕ) (p : Polynomial ℂ), ∀ z, f z = p.eval z` — entire but not polynomial
- `IsNonLinear(f)` := `¬∃ (a b : ℂ), ∀ z, f z = a * z + b` — not affine

The transcendence condition is strictly stronger than non-linearity: every transcendental function is non-linear, but not conversely ($z^2$ is non-linear but polynomial).
mathContext: An entire function has a power series $f(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n z^n$ converging on all of $\mathbb{C}$. It is transcendental iff infinitely many $a_n \neq 0$. The `Differentiable ℂ f` condition in Mathlib is equivalent to holomorphicity by Cauchy-Riemann.

title: ℚ is Countable Dense (Proved)
content:
`IsCountableDense(S)` := `S.Countable ∧ Dense S`.

`rationals_countable_dense` (**proved**): $\mathbb{Q}$ is countable and dense in $\mathbb{R}$. The proof is a direct two-line application of `Set.countable_range` and `Rat.denseRange_ratCast` — two fundamental Mathlib facts.

This is the only non-trivial verified theorem in the formalization (everything else is either a definition or derived from axioms).
mathContext: $\mathbb{Q}$ is represented as `Set.range (↑· : ℚ → ℝ)` — the image of the canonical coercion. Density means every open interval $(a, b) \subset \mathbb{R}$ contains a rational, i.e., $\overline{\mathbb{Q}} = \mathbb{R}$.

title: The Erdős and General Questions
content:
Four definitions formalizing the problem:

- `PreservesRationality(f)`: $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}, (\exists q \in \mathbb{Q}, q = x) \Leftrightarrow (\exists q \in \mathbb{Q}, q = f(x))$
- `MapsSetToSet(f, A, B)`: $\forall x, x \in A \Leftrightarrow f(x) \in B$
- `ErdosQuestion`: $\exists$ entire non-linear $f$ preserving rationality
- `GeneralQuestion`: $\forall$ countable dense $A, B$, $\exists$ entire $f$ with $f(A) = B$

The `GeneralQuestion` strictly implies `ErdosQuestion` (take $A = B = \mathbb{Q}$).
mathContext: The rationality-preservation condition $f(x) \in \mathbb{Q} \Leftrightarrow x \in \mathbb{Q}$ is formalized via the coercion $\mathbb{Q} \hookrightarrow \mathbb{R}$ and existential quantification, since Lean represents rationals and reals as distinct types.

title: Barth-Schneider Theorem (1970) — Axiomatized
content:
Two axioms encoding the Barth-Schneider theorem:

1. `barth_schneider_1970` (axiom): For all countable dense $A, B \subset \mathbb{R}$, $\exists$ transcendental entire $f$ with $z \in A \Leftrightarrow f(z) \in B$ on the reals.

2. `barth_schneider_monotone` (axiom): Same, but additionally $f|_{\mathbb{R}}$ is strictly monotone.

The original construction uses Weierstrass products: enumerate $A = \{a_n\}$, $B = \{b_n\}$, and build $f$ as an infinite product forcing $f(a_n) = b_n$ while maintaining entireness. The monotonicity requires more care in ordering the interpolation points.
mathContext: The construction produces $f(z) = \lim_{n \to \infty} P_n(z)$ where each $P_n$ is a polynomial interpolating the first $n$ pairs $(a_i, b_i)$, with corrections via Weierstrass factors $E_p(z/z_n)$ to ensure convergence on $\mathbb{C}$.

title: The Answer: YES (Proved from Axioms)
content:
`erdos_question_affirmative` (**proved**): The answer is YES.

The proof instantiates `barth_schneider_1970` with $A = B = \text{Set.range}(\uparrow \cdot : \mathbb{Q} \to \mathbb{R})$, applying `rationals_countable_dense`. It then shows transcendental $\Rightarrow$ non-linear by contradiction: if $f(z) = az + b$, encode this as the polynomial $C(b) + C(a) \cdot X$, contradicting transcendence.

`general_question_affirmative` (**proved**): Follows immediately by unwrapping `barth_schneider_1970` and extracting the `IsEntire` component from `IsTranscendental`.
mathContext: The transcendental $\Rightarrow$ non-linear step: any affine function $az + b$ equals $\text{eval}_z(b + aX)$, a degree-1 polynomial. So $f$ would satisfy $\exists n, p, \forall z, f(z) = p.\text{eval}(z)$, contradicting `IsTranscendental`. Uses `ring_nf` to simplify $a \cdot z + b = (b + a \cdot X).\text{eval}(z)$.

title: Complex Extension (1971)
content:
`barth_schneider_complex` (axiom): For countable dense $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{C}$, $\exists$ transcendental entire $f$ with $z \in A \Leftrightarrow f(z) \in B$.

This is a substantial generalization: $\mathbb{C}$ has richer topology than $\mathbb{R}$ (simply connected, algebraically closed), so the interpolation argument requires different techniques to handle the two-dimensional dense set.
mathContext: Countable dense subsets of $\mathbb{C}$ include $\mathbb{Q}[i] = \{a + bi : a, b \in \mathbb{Q}\}$ and $\overline{\mathbb{Q}} \cap \mathbb{C}$ (algebraic numbers). The axiom states the result for arbitrary such sets.

title: Why Polynomials Fail
content:
`no_polynomial_works` (axiom): No polynomial of degree $> 1$ preserves rationality bidirectionally.

The argument: if $p \in \mathbb{R}[x]$ with $\deg p > 1$ and $p(\mathbb{Q}) \subseteq \mathbb{Q}$, then $p$ must have rational coefficients (by evaluating at $0, 1, 2, \ldots$). But a degree-$d$ rational polynomial $p(x) - r = 0$ has at most $d$ roots, so most irrational preimages of rationals exist: $\exists x \notin \mathbb{Q}$ with $p(x) \in \mathbb{Q}$, breaking the biconditional.
mathContext: For $p(x) = x^2$: $p(\sqrt{2}) = 2 \in \mathbb{Q}$ but $\sqrt{2} \notin \mathbb{Q}$. This is the simplest counterexample. More generally, $p^{-1}(\mathbb{Q})$ is dense but strictly larger than $\mathbb{Q}$ for any $\deg p > 1$.

title: Summary: Problem SOLVED
content:
Three theorems wrap up the formalization:

- `erdos_226_summary` (**proved**): `ErdosQuestion ∧ GeneralQuestion`
- `erdos_226` := `erdos_question_affirmative` (alias)
- `erdos_226_answer` (**proved**): $\exists$ entire transcendental $f$ preserving rationality — the most explicit statement

**Score**: 4 axioms (Barth-Schneider real/complex, monotone version, no-polynomial), 1 verified theorem (`rationals_countable_dense`), 3 derived theorems, 0 sorries.
mathContext: The `erdos_226_answer` theorem provides the strongest formulation: $\exists f : \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}$, `IsEntire f` $\wedge$ `IsTranscendental f` $\wedge$ $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}, x \in \mathbb{Q} \Leftrightarrow f(x) \in \mathbb{Q}$.
